units.text: An Answer That Comes with Receipts

Imagine an assistant that says not only “here is the conclusion,” but also “here are the document, the passage, the calculation, and the limits within which the conclusion is supported.” It does not ask us to trust its personality. It offers something that can be inspected.
We will call this result an answer with a verification dossier. It is not a universal certificate of truth. It is a way to reduce the distance between a claim and the reason we accept it.
One Sentence Contains Several Obligations

Take a fictional claim: “The pilot program reduced average processing time by 40% and improved safety.” The first part requires two comparable time values and a calculation. The second requires a definition of safety and relevant measurements. A source supporting the first part does not automatically support the second.

FActScore, introduced by Min and colleagues, decomposes texts into atomic factual claims and evaluates their support by sources. This approach helps with finer evaluations than a global verdict on a paragraph. But the proportion of supported claims does not guarantee the text’s completeness or automatically detect a biased selection of true facts. [31]
A summary can contain only true claims and still omit the decisive cost. That is why we need two different checks: is what is asserted supported? And was what needed to be included actually included?
The Path of a Claim

In a workflow proposed here, documents receive an identity and version. The system extracts verifiable statements, links them to passages, and marks whether support is explicit, inferred, or absent. Calculations are executed separately. Contradictions between sources are preserved rather than smoothed into a comfortable conclusion.

Then an evaluator checks the meaning of the connection. It is not enough for the source to exist and contain the same words. It must support the precise claim, with the same population, period, and conditions. In ALCE, Gao and colleagues treat citation quality as a distinct problem alongside other dimensions of the answer. A rich bibliography is not equivalent to a well-supported argument. [32]

Finally, the result can say: “Four claims are directly supported; one is an inference; for one, I found no data.” This wording may be less spectacular than a perfectly smooth synthesis. But it lets users make an informed decision.
A Complete Example, Without Real Documents

Suppose we receive two fictional documents about a project. Document A records that an activity took ten hours. Document B shows that, after a tool was introduced, the same activity took six hours across ten attempts. We have no comparison group and do not know whether the difficulty of the attempts remained identical.

The system can arithmetically verify the four-hour decrease and the 40% reduction from ten. It cannot infer from these data alone that the tool caused the entire difference. It cannot infer that the firm can shorten all deadlines by 40%. It cannot infer that errors decreased if we have no measure of errors.

An acceptable answer would distinguish the levels: “In the supplied data, reported duration fell from ten to six hours. The calculated reduction is 40%. Causal attribution and generalization to other tasks are not established.” This is not a timid answer. It is an answer that does not expand its own competence.

Mechanization is already possible for part of this process: checking numbers, identifying passages, executing the formula, detecting the absence of a measure. Assessing the comparability of tasks may require a specialist and further information. The system’s strength also lies in sending this precise question, rather than generic text, to the person who can answer it.
A Correct Summary Can Still Be Unfair

Suppose a report describes ten minor advantages and one major disadvantage. A summary that preserves five advantages and omits the disadvantage can have every sentence correct. The problem is selection.

To mechanize completeness better, we can define mandatory categories in advance: results, costs, adverse effects, limits, contradictions. We can request a second process that explicitly seeks omitted information in these categories. We can check critical claims individually without diluting them into an average.

But importance cannot always be fully formalized. In a social conflict, choosing what deserves emphasis involves values and perspective. The system should state its selection criterion and allow it to be challenged, rather than presenting the summary as the only possible neutral representation.
Provenance Is Not Truth

A registry can preserve who supplied a document, which version was used, and whether the material was altered. This infrastructure is valuable. It does not, however, turn content into fact. If a document asserts something false, preserving it impeccably helps us demonstrate what was said, not that what was said was true.

The same reasoning applies to a hash, a signature, or a blockchain record: confirming integrity or origin does not on its own resolve the relationship between a claim and the world. The book is making a logical distinction here, not proposing a cryptographic product. An error durably recorded can become an error with an excellent history.
The Dossier Must Also Protect the Person

Not all evidence needs to be published in full. Documents may contain personal data, confidential information, or health details. A verification process must provide for proportionate access, retention of the minimum necessary, and separation between the public explanation and sensitive material.

Transparency is not synonymous with total exposure. A responsible system must allow auditing without turning users’ lives into raw material for a public demonstration. Verifiability and confidentiality are goals that must be designed together, not negotiated only after an incident.
